## Overview

The Anlo Ewe are a sub-group of the Ewe people, inhabiting southern Togo, southern Benin, southwest Nigeria, and south-eastern parts of the Volta Region of Ghana. The Ewe number approximately 6 million people, with a majority located in the entire southern half of Togo and southwest Benin. The Anlo Ewe speak Anlogbe, a dialect of the Ewe language within the Gbe language cluster. They are a patrilineal society governed by a hierarchical, centralized authority. Their cultural life includes clan-based organization, royal and military institutions, traditional religious practices, funerary ceremonies, colorful dance, and drumming performances.

## Material culture

### Clothing & dress

The sources mention daily clothes-washing activities in the account of the Ewe escape from Notsie, and they state that non-members attending Afa rituals must wear white clothing. Funeral costs include burial clothes.

### Architecture

The sources state that the people lived in Notsie, Togo, a city circumscribed by a large sacred wall that became a barrier to escape. They also mention villages in the coastal regions of Togo and Benin and settlements in the south-eastern parts of the Volta Region of Ghana. No house forms, building materials, roof types, or architectural decorations are documented.

## Music & performance

Anlo-Ewe funerals are described as events likely to involve colorful performances by dance and drumming groups. These performances may be lively and spectacular when the deceased was an honorable and involved member of the community. Distant family members may commission performances months after death if they could not attend the funeral.

The sources also describe performances as central to devotional activities for Afa, an astral god of divination and the younger brother of Yewe. Members and non-members celebrate Afa together, although a non-member must wear white clothing and cannot dance next to a member unless at a funeral.

## Dance & theatre

The sources document dance in connection with Afa devotion and funerals. Afa members and non-members celebrate together, but a non-member cannot dance next to a member unless at a funeral, and ritual rules govern participation. Anlo-Ewe funerals can include lively and spectacular dance performances, especially when the deceased was an honorable and involved member of the community.

## Festivals & rituals

They do describe religious initiation, funerals, and lineage ceremonies.

Yewe is the god of thunder and lightning. After initiation under Yewe, a person receives a Yewe name at a graduation ceremony. The person’s old name becomes taboo, and someone who uses it can be brought before a council of priests and sentenced to pay a large fine. Afa members do not receive new names and keep their birth names.

Traditional funerals incorporate several events over a month. On Amedigbe, the body, previously preserved with herbs, is buried, usually two to three days after death. Ndinamegbe is the day after burial, when principal mourners are received. Nudogbe is a wake-keeping day four to six days after burial. On Yofogbe, the day after wake-keeping, lineage rituals are performed, and family members receive gifts and donations for funeral expenses. Three days later, on Akontawogbe, donations are counted. Several days after Akontawogbe, on Xomefewogbe, the final funeral cost is calculated. In a more modernized and mobile society, funerals usually take place over a single weekend, sometimes several weeks after death.

## Foodways

The sources mention food and alcohol among the costs of an Anlo funeral, together with the provision of accommodations for distant guests.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources preserve an account of the Ewe escape from Notsie. After Togbe Agorkoli ruled oppressively, the people consulted the hidden elder Tegli and planned their escape by weakening the sacred wall through daily clothes-washing activities. Tegli drew the “Sword of Liberation,” summoned the gods, and pierced the wall while proclaiming: “O Mawuga Kitikata, ʋuʋɔ na mi ne miadogo, azɔ adzo” (“Oh great God Kitikata, open the door for us so that we walk through).” During the escape, the people walked backwards and separated so that King Agorkoli could not trace them.

## Language & religion

Anlogbe is the self-name of the Anlo Ewe language, which is a dialect of the Ewe language and belongs to the Gbe language cluster. Traditionally, the Anlo-Ewe recognize one Supreme God, Mawuga Kitikata, or Mawu. Mawu is described as synonymous with the Christian Almighty God and as all-powerful and everywhere at once. Because of this belief in divine omnipresence, there are no shrines or devotional ceremonies dedicated to Mawu; religious practice instead centers on lower-level divinities, including Yewe, Afa, Eda, Nana, and Mami Wata. Christianity has been accepted throughout Anlo Ewe land, while a minority still practices traditional Vodun beliefs.
